subject: music
title: Riot grrrl: Bikini Kill, zines and "girls to the front" (1990–1996)
dek: In the summer of 1991 a handful of young women in Olympia, Washington, and Washington, D.C., decided that punk, which claimed to be the music of rebellion, had left them standing at the back of the room. They started bands, photocopied zines, held meetings and called it riot grrrl. Within two years the movement had chapters across America, a sister scene in England and a media frenzy it tried to shut down.
era: 1990 to about 1996, with roots in 1970s women's punk and effects into third-wave and fourth-wave feminism
honesty: This lesson keeps to dates, names and events documented in the English Wikipedia articles on riot grrrl, Bikini Kill, Kathleen Hanna, Bratmobile, Heavens to Betsy, Huggy Bear, Sleater-Kinney, Kill Rock Stars, the International Pop Underground Convention, Smells Like Teen Spirit and Shonen Knife, and the Chinese Wikipedia articles on 彭婉如命案, 何春蕤 and 濁水溪公社. Short quotations come from those articles, which cite the original zines, interviews and books. The analysis sections are my own summary, not claims from a single source.

timeline.label: Jigsaw and D.C. discussions
timeline.detail: Tobi Vail starts her zine Jigsaw in Olympia. In Washington, D.C., Sharon Cheslow, Amy Pickering, Cynthia Connolly and Lydia Ely organise group discussions about sexism in the local punk scene.

timeline.label: Bikini Kill forms
timeline.detail: In October, Kathleen Hanna, Tobi Vail, Kathi Wilcox and Billy Karren form Bikini Kill in Olympia. Molly Neuman makes the first issue of the zine Girl Germs over winter break.

timeline.label: Kill Rock Stars founded
timeline.detail: Slim Moon and Tinuviel Sampson start the Kill Rock Stars label in Olympia in February. Its first release is a split spoken-word record by Kathleen Hanna and Slim Moon.

timeline.label: The riot grrrl zine and the first meeting
timeline.detail: In summer, Bikini Kill and Bratmobile are in Washington, D.C. Neuman and Allison Wolfe make the first riot grrrl zine, and Hanna and Jenny Toomey organise the first meeting at the Positive Force house in Arlington, Virginia.

timeline.label: Girl Night
timeline.detail: On 20 August the International Pop Underground Convention opens in Olympia with an almost all-female bill, later known as Girl Night.

timeline.label: Riot Grrrl Convention and media blackout
timeline.detail: The first Riot Grrrl Convention is held in Washington, D.C., from 31 July to 2 August. After condescending coverage in Newsweek, USA Today and others, Hanna calls for a media blackout.

timeline.label: Pussy Whipped and the UK tour
timeline.detail: Bikini Kill release Pussy Whipped in September, including Rebel Girl. Huggy Bear are thrown out of the studio of The Word in February, and the two bands tour Britain together.

timeline.label: Splits and Sleater-Kinney
timeline.detail: Bratmobile, Heavens to Betsy and Huggy Bear break up. Corin Tucker and Carrie Brownstein form Sleater-Kinney in Olympia.

timeline.label: The end of the first wave
timeline.detail: Bikini Kill release Reject All American in 1996 and break up in 1997 after a last show in Tokyo.

fun_fact.title: Kurt smells like Teen Spirit
fun_fact.text: The title of Nirvana's biggest song came from a riot grrrl. Kathleen Hanna and Tobi Vail, who was then Kurt Cobain's girlfriend, found a deodorant called Teen Spirit at a grocery store and thought the name was funny. Later Hanna wrote 'Kurt smells like Teen Spirit' in marker on Cobain's wall. Cobain read it as a revolutionary slogan, since they had been talking about anarchism and punk, and said he did not know about the deodorant until months after Smells Like Teen Spirit came out. The song went on to sell more than 13 million copies, while Bikini Kill's own anthem Rebel Girl, released on an independent label, never charted at all.

sections.title: Before riot grrrl: women in punk, and punk without women

blocks.text: Women had been central to punk from the start. In London in the late 1970s, Poly Styrene of X-Ray Spex, Siouxsie Sioux, the Slits and the Raincoats made records that sounded nothing like male rock. In America, Joan Jett had come out of the Runaways, and in the 1980s Kim Gordon of Sonic Youth and Kim Deal of the Pixies showed that a woman could play bass, sing and shape a band's sound. Kathleen Hanna later said that just knowing Gordon existed made her feel less alone. A 1982 film, Ladies and Gentlemen, The Fabulous Stains, about a fictional teenage girl punk band, also became a cult favourite among future riot grrrls.

But by the late 1980s, American punk had changed. Hardcore, the fast and aggressive style that grew in Washington, D.C., Los Angeles and elsewhere, made the front of the stage a mosh pit where young men slammed into each other. Women who wanted to stand near the band had to fight their way in and risked being groped. Very few women played in the bands. Tobi Vail wrote in her zine Jigsaw that she felt 'completely left out', partly because 'punk rock is for and by boys mostly'.

Two small scenes were already preparing an answer. Olympia, a small state capital with a liberal arts college called The Evergreen State College, had a strong do-it-yourself culture: K Records, run by Calvin Johnson and Candice Pedersen, the community radio station KAOS, and the feminist art space Girl City. In Washington, D.C., where Ian MacKaye's Dischord Records had made the city a hardcore centre, women such as Sharon Cheslow, Amy Pickering, Cynthia Connolly and Lydia Ely began meeting in 1988 to talk about sexism in the scene, and published the results in the punk magazine Maximum Rock 'n' Roll.

sections.title: Olympia and D.C.: zines, bands and the first meeting

blocks.text: A zine is a small, self-published magazine, usually written by hand or typed, cut and pasted, and photocopied in a few dozen or few hundred copies. Punk had used zines since the 1970s, and the women of Olympia used them to say things that no newspaper or music magazine would print. Tobi Vail started Jigsaw in 1988, and Donna Dresch started Chainsaw around the same time. In Jigsaw, Vail wrote about 'angry grrls', combining the word girls with a growl.

Kathleen Hanna, born in 1968 in Portland, Oregon, was studying at Evergreen. She volunteered at SafePlace, an Olympia shelter for survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault, where she did counselling and gave talks in high schools. She first worked as a spoken-word performer, but the writer Kathy Acker told her that nobody went to spoken-word shows and she should start a band. Hanna read Jigsaw, admired it, sought out Vail, and in October 1990 they formed Bikini Kill with the bassist Kathi Wilcox and the guitarist Billy Karren.

At the same time, two University of Oregon students, Allison Wolfe from Olympia and Molly Neuman from D.C., were making their own zine, Girl Germs, and forming the band Bratmobile. A friend, Jen Smith, wrote to Wolfe: 'We need to start a girl RIOT!' In the summer of 1991 both bands were in Washington, D.C., where riots in the Mount Pleasant neighbourhood had broken out that spring. Neuman and Wolfe put out a new zine, and Neuman titled it riot grrrl. The name of the movement comes from that photocopied sheet.

That summer Hanna and Jenny Toomey, who ran the indie label Simple Machines, organised the first riot grrrl meeting at the house of the activist group Positive Force in Arlington, Virginia. Young women sat in a room and talked about sexism in punk, about abuse, and about their bodies. Weekly meetings like this, run without leaders, became as important to riot grrrl as the concerts.

sections.title: Girl Night at the International Pop Underground Convention

blocks.text: From 20 to 25 August 1991, K Records held the International Pop Underground Convention in Olympia, a festival of independent bands. Its poster invited, among others, 'the editors of every angry grrrl zine'. The first night, organised by Lois Maffeo, the KAOS DJ Michelle Noel and Margaret Doherty, was an almost all-female bill called 'Love Rock Revolution Girl Style Now!', later simply Girl Night.

The line-up included Bratmobile, Heavens to Betsy playing their first show (Corin Tucker on guitar and vocals, Tracy Sawyer on drums), 7 Year Bitch, Jean Smith of Mecca Normal, the Spinanes, Rose Melberg, Nikki McClure, and two side projects of Kathleen Hanna. Many of the women had only known each other through letters, zines and phone calls. Girl Night was where the network met in person. Later in the week the convention featured Bikini Kill, Fugazi, L7, Nation of Ulysses, Unwound and many others.

A month later, in September 1991, Nirvana, a band from Aberdeen, Washington, whose members were friends of the Olympia scene, released Nevermind on a major label. Seattle 'grunge' became a global fashion almost overnight. Riot grrrl grew up in exactly the same place at exactly the same moment, but it took the opposite path and stayed underground.

sections.title: Bikini Kill and "girls to the front"

blocks.text: Bikini Kill's music was simple, loud and fast: Vail's pounding drums, Wilcox's bass, Karren's guitar, and Hanna's voice moving from a sneer to a scream. What made the band different was what happened in the room. Hanna asked the young men at the front to move to the sides or the back so that girls could stand near the stage. The band handed out lyric sheets so the audience could read words about rape, incest and harassment that would otherwise be lost in the noise. Hanna sometimes jumped into the crowd herself to remove men who heckled or attacked her. 'Girls to the front' became the movement's best-known slogan.

The hostility was real. Hanna remembered that people threw chains at the band's heads, and that on one night men would shout 'take it off' while the next night crowds of girls would sing along to every word. From 1992 Hanna wrote words such as 'slut' on her stomach in marker before shows, taking an insult used against women and displaying it on purpose, in the tradition of feminist performance art.

Bikini Kill released a demo cassette, Revolution Girl Style Now, in 1991 and an EP on Kill Rock Stars in 1992. Their debut album Pussy Whipped came out in September 1993. It included Rebel Girl, a song about admiring another girl ('that girl thinks she's the queen of the neighborhood'), which became the anthem of the movement. Joan Jett, whom Hanna regarded as a forerunner of riot grrrl, produced a single version of the song. Rolling Stone dismissed the album as 'yowling and moronic nag-unto-vomit tantrums'. Bikini Kill released Reject All American in 1996 and broke up in 1997.

A typed Bikini Kill flyer answered the question 'What is riot grrrl?' with a list of reasons, each beginning with 'Because'. One reads: 'Because we girls want to create mediums that speak to US. We are tired of boy band after boy band, boy zine after boy zine, boy punk after boy punk after boy.' This list, often called the Riot Grrrl Manifesto, is the clearest statement of what the movement wanted: not only equal rights in law, but space to make culture.

Riot grrrl was never one sound. Bratmobile played short, jangly, sarcastic punk songs; their album Pottymouth appeared on Kill Rock Stars in 1993. Heavens to Betsy were a duo with a raw, intense sound driven by Corin Tucker's powerful voice. Excuse 17, with Carrie Brownstein and Becca Albee, came from Olympia too. Team Dresch, led by Donna Dresch, joined riot grrrl to queercore, the lesbian and gay punk movement. Slant 6, Emily's Sassy Lime and 7 Year Bitch were also part of the wider scene.

items: Bands: Bikini Kill, Bratmobile, Heavens to Betsy, Excuse 17, Team Dresch, Slant 6, Emily's Sassy Lime, Huggy Bear, Skinned Teen.
Labels: K Records and Kill Rock Stars in Olympia, Simple Machines in Arlington, Chainsaw (Donna Dresch's label), and Catcall and Wiiija in England.

Zines: Jigsaw (Tobi Vail), Girl Germs (Molly Neuman and Allison Wolfe), riot grrrl, Bikini Kill, Chainsaw (Donna Dresch), GUNK (Ramdasha Bikceem), Slant (Mimi Thi Nguyen) and Bamboo Girl (Sabrina Margarita Alcantara-Tan).

blocks.text: The zines mattered as much as the records. They described experiences of sexual abuse, eating disorders, racism, homophobia and depression in a 'privately public' voice: intimate writing that was mailed to strangers. Ramdasha Bikceem, a Black teenager from New Jersey, started GUNK in 1990 when she was 15, and wrote about how police would remember her face more clearly than those of her white friends. In 1992 Erika Reinstein and May Summer started Riot Grrrl Press in Washington, D.C., to copy and distribute zines. From July 31 to August 2, 1992, the first Riot Grrrl Convention in D.C. held concerts and workshops on rape, sexuality, racism, domestic violence and self-defence, and also on practical skills like running a soundboard and laying out a zine.

Men were part of the story too. Billy Karren played guitar in Bikini Kill, Calvin Johnson and Slim Moon released riot grrrl records on their labels, and Kurt Cobain was a fan of the Slits and the Raincoats. But the movement's point was that women would decide what happened in their own scene.

sections.title: Huggy Bear and the English scene

blocks.text: Riot grrrl reached England through letters and zines. Liz Naylor, a former writer for the Manchester zine City Fun, met Kathi Wilcox by chance while travelling in Europe in 1991, and Wilcox later sent her music and copies of Jigsaw and riot grrrl. Naylor founded the label Catcall and managed Huggy Bear, a band from Brighton and London that formed in 1991 and called themselves 'girl-boy revolutionaries', because the band included both women and men.

On 14 February 1993, Huggy Bear played their single Her Jazz on The Word, a late-night Channel 4 programme. They stayed in the studio to watch the next item, a report on models called the Barbi Twins, and they and their fans began shouting at the presenter Terry Christian. They were thrown out of the studio. The music paper Melody Maker put the incident on its cover and compared it with the Sex Pistols' notorious 1976 television interview with Bill Grundy.

In 1993 Huggy Bear and Bikini Kill released a split album, Our Troubled Youth / Yeah Yeah Yeah Yeah, and toured Britain together. The filmmaker Lucy Thane followed the tour with borrowed cameras and made the documentary It Changed My Life: Bikini Kill in the UK. Skinned Teen, a London band whose members were about 14 when they formed in 1992, appear in it. Huggy Bear had promised to exist for only three years, and they kept that promise: their last show was in December 1994.

sections.title: The media blackout and the criticism

blocks.text: In 1992 the mainstream press discovered riot grrrl. Newsweek described it as 'feminism with a loud happy face dotting the i', and USA Today wrote that 'from hundreds of once pink, frilly bedrooms comes the young feminist revolution'. Reporters focused on the barrettes, the baby-doll dresses and the words written on skin, and rarely on what the women said about sexual abuse. Corin Tucker later said the media 'refused to do serious interviews with us' and took their writing out of context. Kathleen Hanna asked members to stop talking to the mainstream press, a decision known as the media blackout. Tobi Vail wrote in 1994 that Bikini Kill had never called themselves a riot grrrl band and were not leaders of the movement.

The blackout protected the movement from being turned into a fashion, but it also meant others defined it. The term 'riot grrrl' was attached to almost any band with a woman in it, including Hole, Babes in Toyland and L7, who had never used it. L7's Donita Sparks said she cheered when an Italian poster simply called them 'Rock from the USA'. Courtney Love of Hole criticised riot grrrls for being too quick to be offended and for excusing poor musicianship.

A more serious criticism came from inside. In 1993 Ramdasha Bikceem wrote in GUNK that riot grrrl was 'growing very closed to a very few i.e. white middle class punk girls'. Mimi Thi Nguyen and Sabrina Margarita Alcantara-Tan wrote about the movement from the perspective of Asian American girls, and in 1997 Nguyen published the compilation zine Evolution of a Race Riot. In the same year, the Black punk musician Tamar-kali Brown started Sista Grrrl in New York with Simi Stone, Honeychild Coleman and Maya Sokora, a series of shows by and for Black women in punk. These critiques belong to the history of intersectionality, the idea that sexism is experienced differently depending on race and class.

items: What riot grrrl changed: it treated the concert as a political space and asked who gets to stand at the front.
It made the personal into public writing, decades before blogs and social media, through zines sent by post.
It insisted that girls make culture instead of only consuming it, which is the same do-it-yourself idea punk had promised but not delivered to women.
Its limits: a mostly white, middle-class base, and a refusal to speak to the press that left others to tell its story.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: In the same years, the second-wave legal agenda of the 1970s was giving way to what the writer Rebecca Walker in 1992 called the third wave of feminism, and riot grrrl is often treated as its musical voice. In October 1991 the Anita Hill hearings in the United States Senate, where Hill testified that the Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas had sexually harassed her, made sexual harassment a national subject. Later in the decade in Britain, the mainstream answer to girl anger was the Spice Girls' 'girl power', which many riot grrrls saw as a commercial version of their own ideas with the politics removed.

In Japan, the Osaka trio Shonen Knife, formed in 1981 by Naoko Yamano, her sister Atsuko Yamano and Michie Nakatani, had become a favourite of the American indie underground. Kurt Cobain invited them to open for Nirvana on a European tour in 1991 and said that seeing them live turned him into 'a hysterical nine-year-old girl at a Beatles concert'. Their songs about cookies and banana chips were the opposite of riot grrrl's anger, but they showed that an all-woman rock band could have an international audience.

In Taiwan, the early 1990s were the first years after martial law ended in 1987. Student radicals at National Taiwan University formed the noisy, provocative band 濁水溪公社 (Loh Tsui-kweh Commune) around 1989–1990, and their first album appeared in 1995. On 22 May 1994 the Women's Coalition (女人連線) held a march in Taipei against sexual harassment, and the professor 何春蕤 (Josephine Ho) led the chant 'I want orgasms, not sexual harassment' (我要性高潮，不要性騷擾), which shocked the press much as Hanna's written-on body shocked American reporters.

Then on 30 November 1996, 彭婉如 (Peng Wan-ru), a former secretary-general of the Awakening Foundation (婦女新知基金會) and head of the Democratic Progressive Party's women's department, disappeared after getting into a taxi in Kaohsiung and was found murdered. The case shocked Taiwan. On 31 December 1996 the Legislative Yuan passed the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act (性侵害犯罪防治法), which took effect on 22 January 1997, and the Peng Wan-ru Foundation was set up in May 1997. Riot grrrl's zines and workshops on rape and self-defence and Taiwan's laws on women's personal safety came out of the same decade's anger about violence against women, by very different routes: one through punk culture, the other through organisations and legislation.

By the mid-1990s the first wave of riot grrrl bands had broken up. The most lasting band of the movement formed from its remains: Corin Tucker of Heavens to Betsy and Carrie Brownstein of Excuse 17 started Sleater-Kinney in Olympia in 1994, naming it after a local road. With the drummer Janet Weiss from 1997, they released seven albums between 1995 and 2005, including Call the Doctor and Dig Me Out, and the critic Greil Marcus named them America's best rock band in 2001. They reunited in 2014. Brownstein later co-created the television comedy Portlandia.

Kathleen Hanna formed Julie Ruin, a solo bedroom-recording project, and then the electronic feminist band Le Tigre with Johanna Fateman and Sadie Benning (later JD Samson). She left Le Tigre in 2005 because of illness, later diagnosed as late-stage Lyme disease, a story told in the 2013 documentary The Punk Singer. Bikini Kill reunited briefly in 2017 and toured from 2019.

Riot grrrl also became an archive and an inspiration. Since 2010 the Fales Library at New York University has held the Riot Grrrl Collection, with zines and letters donated by Hanna, Neuman, Wolfe, Bikceem and others. Sara Marcus's 2010 book Girls to the Front was the first published history of the movement. In 2012 the Russian group Pussy Riot, who described themselves as twenty-first-century riot grrrls, were convicted of hooliganism for a protest performance in Moscow's Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. And every girls' rock camp, every feminist zine fair and every 'girls to the front' sign at a gig today descends from those meetings in 1991.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Riot grrrl refused to talk to the mainstream media so that its message would not be twisted, but this left others to define it. If you were running a small feminist project today, such as a shop that gives its profits to women's organisations, when would you accept attention from big media or brands, and when would you say no?
